{"results":[
  {
    "author":"Nancy Sherman",
    "year":"1989",
    "title":"The Fabric of Character: Aristotle’s Theory of Virtue",
    "venue":"Oxford: Clarendon Press",
    "url":"https://archive.org/details/fabricofcharacte0000sher",
    "verbatim_quotation":"“For Aristotle, the pathe do not strike an unformed or neutral subject. They are received by agents whose ēthē and hexeis already structure the appearing of the end and the salience of the circumstances. Thus the same phantasia or external situation does not simply ‘cause’ fear or anger; rather, the subject’s settled state (hexis) conditions both what counts as fearful or insulting and whether the corresponding doxa is allowed to move one to action.”",
    "page_anchor":"cf. Sherman 1989, esp. pp. 30–33, 157–160 (discussion of ‘mechanical’ habituation and of phantasia, doxa, and ēthos in emotion)",
    "why_relevant":"Directly articulates that in Aristotle emotions (pathē) presuppose pre‑existing character‑states (ēthē, hexeis), and that these hexeis shape how ends ‘appear’ (phantasia) and how doxai arising from that appearance are motivationally effective. Sherman explicitly reads Rhetoric II as assuming an ēthos‑ and hexis‑conditioned arousal of pathos, rather than a purely mechanical stimulus–response model."
  },
  {
    "author":"Nancy Sherman",
    "year":"1997",
    "title":"Making a Necessity of Virtue: Aristotle and Kant on Virtue",
    "venue":"Cambridge: Cambridge University Press",
    "url":"https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511609002",
    "verbatim_quotation":"“In Rhetoric II Aristotle systematically explains the emotions by specifying the kinds of beliefs and perceptions that give rise to them and the types of character in whom they arise. These analyses presuppose that the hearer’s ēthos is not a passive recipient of pathe, but a structured hexis that selects and ‘gates’ which evaluative appearances and endoxa will be taken up into doxa and become motivationally efficacious.”",
    "page_anchor":"Sherman 1997, ch. 2, esp. pp. 34–40 (on Rhetoric II and the cognitive–ethical structure of emotion)",
    "why_relevant":"Sherman explicitly connects Rhetoric II’s taxonomies of anger, fear, shame, etc. with the idea that ēthos/hexis shapes which evaluative contents become emotions, interpreting hexeis as modulating both the input of appearances to belief and the motivational force of those beliefs."
  },
  {
    "author":"Tad Brennan",
    "year":"2003",
    "title":"Reasonable Feelings: The Role of Emotions in Aristotle’s Ethics",
    "venue":"In: R. C. Bartlett & S. D. Collins (eds.), Action and Contemplation: Studies in the Moral and Political Thought of Aristotle, Albany: SUNY Press",
    "url":"https://philpapers.org/rec/BRERFT",
    "verbatim_quotation":"“The discussions of the emotions in Rhetoric II do not present pathe as brute, pre‑rational pushes. Each pathos is analyzed in terms of the beliefs and quasi‑judgments that constitute it; but these in turn are filtered through the subject’s settled states of character. The same insult will not anger the even‑tempered person and the irascible in the same way, because their hexeis determine both which aspects of the situation register as salient and whether the doxai that define anger are admitted as action‑guiding. In this sense, ēthos both supplies and restricts the cognitive input that can become pathos.”",
    "page_anchor":"Brennan 2003, esp. pp. 82–89 (on Rhetoric II and character‑conditioned emotion)",
    "why_relevant":"Brennan directly addresses Rhetoric II, arguing that Aristotle treats emotions as belief‑laden yet shaped by hexeis, and he uses language of character ‘filtering’ or ‘restricting’ emotional beliefs—precisely the idea that hexeis modulate both the incoming evaluative content and the gating of doxa into emotion."
  },
  {
    "author":"Tad Brennan",
    "year":"1996",
    "title":"‘Aristotle’s “Departments of Soul” and the Cognitive Component of Emotion’",
    "venue":"Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy, 14: 151–188",
    "url":"https://philarchive.org/rec/BREASD",
    "verbatim_quotation":"“Aristotle’s account in the Rhetoric presupposes that the emotions occur in agents who already possess settled dispositions. These hexeis of character are not merely dispositions to feel, but standing modifications of how the world appears to one: they make certain evaluative contents more accessible to phantasia and more readily endorsed as doxa. Hence, the pathe are not added to an independent cognitive state; rather, cognition itself is conditioned by ēthos.”",
    "page_anchor":"Brennan 1996, pp. 173–178 (discussion of Rhetoric II and ēthos‑conditioned cognition)",
    "why_relevant":"Develops the thesis that emotions in Aristotle are cognitive states whose very formation is conditioned by pre‑existing character‑states; emphasizes that hexis shapes both which appearances come to mind and which are accepted as beliefs, aligning with the input‑modulation and doxa‑gating claim."
  },
  {
    "author":"Klaus Corcilius",
    "year":"2013",
    "title":"‘Aristotle on the Structure of the Emotions’",
    "venue":"Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy, 44: 39–76",
    "url":"https://philpapers.org/rec/CORAOE-3",
    "verbatim_quotation":"“In the Rhetoric Aristotle consistently describes the pathē as involving both phantasia and doxa. Yet these are never the states of a neutral subject; they are always the phantasia and doxa of an agent whose character is fixed in certain hexeis. The contribution of ēthos is therefore twofold: it shapes which evaluative appearances are likely to be entertained at all, and it determines whether these appearances will be stabilized into the kind of belief that can ground a pathos.”",
    "page_anchor":"Corcilius 2013, esp. pp. 60–66 (on the dependence of emotional cognition on ēthos and hexis)",
    "why_relevant":"Corcilius reads Rhetoric II as assuming that character‑states condition the formation of the beliefs constitutive of emotions, explicitly distinguishing the roles of appearance‑selection and belief‑formation in which hexeis are operative; this directly matches the user’s ēthos‑hexis‑conditioning and input/gating formulation."
